title: Digital vs. Analog I/O: How the Physical World Becomes a Variable
oneLiner: A limit switch gives a PLC exactly one bit. A pressure transducer gives it a whole range -- but both start as nothing more than a voltage or a current on a wire.
keyTakeaway: Analog I/O conventionally uses 4-20mA, not 0-20mA, specifically so 0mA is never a valid reading -- it's a "live zero," meaning 4mA IS the sensor's zero, so a PLC reading exactly 0mA knows immediately that's a broken wire or a disconnected sensor, not a real measurement.
explanation:
Digital I/O is the simple case: a physical input (a limit switch, a push button, a proximity sensor) is either passing voltage or not -- ON or OFF, a single bit, read directly into the PLC's input image table each scan (see PLCs: How They're Different From a Normal Computer). There's no "in between": either the circuit is complete and the PLC reads 1, or it isn't and the PLC reads 0.

Analog I/O represents a continuous physical quantity -- pressure, temperature, flow, level -- as a continuous electrical signal instead, most commonly a 4-20mA current loop: 4mA represents the sensor's minimum reading (say, 0 PSI), 20mA represents its maximum (say, 100 PSI), and everything in between scales linearly. The PLC's analog input module reads the raw current, and the PLC program (or the module itself) converts it into an engineering value using that same linear scale. Critically, the range starts at 4mA, not 0mA -- a "live zero." That gap between 0 and 4mA isn't wasted: it's reserved specifically so 0mA is never a valid reading. A cut wire, a disconnected sensor, or a dead transmitter all read as 0mA, and because a healthy loop NEVER reports 0, the PLC can immediately flag that as a fault instead of silently treating it as "0 PSI" and potentially making a dangerous decision on bad data.
